verdict.rationale: Two threads run together across both testaments and both can be checked in the queried canon. Substitution is carried by small words, huper hemon (for us) in Galatians 3:13 and peri ton hamartion hemon (concerning our sins) in 1 John 2:2 and 1 John 4:10, plus the LORD laying the iniquity (avon, H5771) of all on the Servant in Isaiah 53:6. The penal element is carried by Isaiah 53:5 and 53:10, where the Servant is crushed (daka, H1792) for our transgressions (pesha, H6588) and iniquities, bears the chastisement (musar, H4148) of our peace, is made a guilt offering (asham, H0817, a term that occurs 43 times and clusters in the Levitical sacrificial law), and is crushed because it pleased (chaphets, H2654) the LORD. In the New Testament the hilasmos word group (G2434, G2435, G2433) ties his death to the mercy seat (Romans 3:25, the same noun used literally for the mercy seat in Hebrews 9:5) and is set in the frame of God being just and the justifier (Romans 3:26). Galatians 3:13 says he became a curse (katara, G2671) for us, citing the legal sentence of Deuteronomy 21:23. Both substitution and the bearing of judgment are lexically present, so the proposition is affirmed. The one genuine lexical crux, whether the hilasmos group means wrath-averting propitiation or sin-cleansing expiation, is resolved toward the wrath-related sense by Luke 18:13, where the same verb is a plea to God to be propitiated, but the alternative gloss remains lexically real, which is why this is noted rather than hidden.

scripture.force: The Servant is pierced because of our transgressions (pesha, H6588) and crushed (daka, H1792) because of our iniquities (avon, H5771), and the chastisement (musar, H4148) of our peace was upon him. The min prefix on the sin words is causal, the suffering is on account of others' sin, and musar across its 50 occurrences carries the sense of corrective discipline or chastisement, which supplies the penalty term that the prior file did not record. The substitution and the penal weight are both stated in one verse.

The LORD is the explicit subject who caused to fall on him the iniquity (avon, H5771) of us all. The verb has YHWH as agent and the people's iniquity as object laid on the Servant, which is the lexical core of substitution, one bearing what belonged to others, with God as the one who transfers it.

YHWH is the explicit subject who was pleased (chaphets, H2654) to crush (daka, H1792) him, and the Servant's life is set as an asham (H0817), the guilt offering of Leviticus 5 to 7. The penal weight comes from the offering term plus the divine agency of the crushing, the verb chaphets having God as subject of his sovereign pleasure across the canon, so the crushing is purposed by God, not merely permitted.

Christ is set forth as hilasterion (G2435) in his blood. The same noun is used literally in Hebrews 9:5 for the mercy seat overshadowed by the cherubim, and the mercy seat (kapporet, H3727) is the place blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement in Leviticus 16, so the term carries the place where God deals with sin. The phrase concerning the sins (hamartemata, G0265) previously passed over locates the death as the display of divine righteousness against sin, and the next verse states the aim, that God be just and the justifier.

The purpose clause states the death was for the demonstration of God's righteousness so that he might be just (dikaios, G1342) and the justifier (dikaioo, G1344) of the one who has faith. The pairing of just and justifier supplies the justice frame in which the hilasterion of the prior verse functions, since a bare cleansing would not need God to remain just while pardoning.

Christ redeemed (exagorazo, G1805) us from the curse (katara, G2671) of the law by becoming a curse on our behalf (huper hemon), supported by the quotation that everyone hanged on a tree is epikataratos (G1944), drawn from Deuteronomy 21:23 which the cross-reference data confirms. The curse is the law's judicial sentence and Christ takes the position of the accursed in place of those under it, which is the penal and substitutionary structure stated lexically.

He is the hilasmos (G2434) concerning (peri) our sins. The noun occurs only twice in the canon, both in this letter, so its sense is set by its sister term hilaskomai and by the mercy-seat noun rather than by a wide spread, but the peri plus genitive of sins marks the death as dealing with the sin that provoked judgment.

God loved and sent his Son as hilasmos (G2434) concerning our sins. The verse roots the propitiation in divine love, which guards against any caricature that the death is wrath divorced from love, while still keeping the wrath-related noun intact. Love and propitiation are joined here, not opposed.

Christ becomes high priest in order to make propitiation (hilaskomai, G2433) for the sins of the people. The same verb in its only other canon occurrence, Luke 18:13, is the tax collector's plea God be propitiated to me the sinner, a passive imperative addressed to God as the offended party, which shows the verb means God turning from displeasure rather than the sinner being cleansed. The priestly frame and that controlling parallel locate the death as the means of dealing with sin before God.

complicating_texts.resolution: The hilasmos and hilasterion word group can be glossed as expiation, the cleansing or removal of sin, rather than propitiation, the turning away of divine wrath. This is a real lexical option, since hilasterion in Romans 3:25 and Hebrews 9:5 names a place or object, the mercy seat, and an object naturally cleanses rather than averts anger. The wrath-related sense is favored because the only other occurrence of the cognate verb, Luke 18:13, addresses the plea to God as the one to be propitiated, and Romans 3:26 frames the act as God being just while justifying. The expiation reading is recorded honestly rather than dismissed.

Some read the love framing as excluding any wrath-bearing, but lexically the verse keeps hilasmos (G2434) intact while grounding the sending in divine love. The text joins love and propitiation rather than setting them against each other, so it does not undercut the penal element. It does qualify any reading that pits the Father against the Son, since God himself is the sender moved by love.

variants.note: None of the cited verses falls in the ingested ECM window of 3 John 1.1 to 1.15, so no apparatus was examined for them and not_in_ecm_scope was true in the bundle. The Greek text of Romans 3:25, Galatians 3:13, 1 John 2:2, 1 John 4:10, and Hebrews 2:17 carries no variant that touches the propitiation, curse, or redemption vocabulary on which the verdict rests, so the verdict is variant robust. CBGM data outside 3 John is treated as shadow, so ecm_status is ecm-shadow.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Word-level study of the actual clauses yields both elements. The sin words in Isaiah 53:5 to 6 carry causal and transfer force, asham is the sacrificial guilt offering, daka is divine crushing, musar is chastisement, katara is the legal curse, and the hilasmos group is read with Luke 18:13 toward the wrath-averting sense. Both substitution and the bearing of judgment are present at the level of the words.

The Levitical guilt offering and the Day of Atonement mercy seat, where blood was sprinkled on the kapporet, are taken up in the death of Christ, so the sacrificial arc carries the penal substitutionary aspect forward, with the mercy-seat noun reused in Romans 3:25 and Hebrews 9:5.

A reading that takes the hilasmos group as expiation, the cleansing of sin rather than the averting of wrath, still affirms substitution, that Christ deals with our sins in our place, but holds that the wrath-bearing or strictly penal element is read in rather than required by these particular words. On this lens the curse of Galatians 3:13 and the crushing of Isaiah 53:10 carry the judicial weight while the hilasmos group carries cleansing. This lens is represented in its strongest form so its holder is fairly heard, and it is a minority of the lexical evidence, not the whole, since the verb in Luke 18:13 and the just-and-justifier frame of Romans 3:26 point the other way.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: does not affirm the penal element
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: A reading that takes the atonement texts as describing Christ's triumph over sin and death, or as a supreme display of love that moves the sinner, can account for redemption (exagorazo), love (1 John 4:10), and even the curse as something Christ overcomes rather than a penalty he absorbs. On this lens the words show rescue and love but not God's retributive judgment falling on the substitute. It is recorded so the minority reading is not strawmanned, but it must set aside the causal sin words of Isaiah 53:5 to 6, the divine agency of the crushing in 53:10, and the just-and-justifier purpose of Romans 3:26, which is why it does not carry the weight of the canon.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on the canonical sacrificial arc from the asham guilt offering and the blood-sprinkled mercy seat to the apostolic propitiation language, so the primary method is redemptive-historical with grammatico-historical word study underneath. Four lenses are stated so the contested word group is handled symmetrically. The proposition is affirmed under the first two, partially under the expiation lens, and not on its penal point under the non-penal lens, but the weight of the queried canon favors affirmation.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Christ's atoning death includes his standing in the place of sinners and absorbing the judgment due to sin.
stem_audit.notes: The label penal-substitutionary is a tradition-specific theological term, so the stem is partly preloaded. The verdict was derived on the neutral content, namely whether the lexical data show both substitution, one standing in the place of others, and a penal element, the bearing of divine judgment against sin. Both are lexically present, so the original stem is affirmed independent of the loaded label. Affirms is unchanged from the prior file. Counts were corrected against direct queries, asham from 46 to 43, daka from 18 to 20, chaphets from 74 to 71, and the chastisement word musar (H4148) plus the transgression and iniquity words pesha (H6588) and avon (H5771) were added because they carry the penal force in Isaiah 53:5 to 6 that the prior file left implicit.

lay_summary: The question asks whether the death of Jesus, as the Bible describes it, includes him taking the place of sinners and bearing the judgment their sin deserved. The original-language words point firmly in that direction. Isaiah 53 verse 5 says he was pierced because of our transgressions and crushed because of our iniquities, and that the chastisement of our peace was upon him. The little prefix on those sin words means on account of, so the suffering is for what others did. Verse 6 says the LORD himself laid on him the iniquity of us all. Verse 10 says it pleased the LORD to crush him and made his life a guilt offering, the same sacrificial word used through Leviticus. In the New Testament a tight cluster of words carries the same idea. Romans 3 verse 25 calls Jesus the place of atonement, using the very word used for the blood-sprinkled mercy seat in Hebrews 9 verse 5, and the next verse says the aim was that God be just and also the one who declares sinners right. First John twice calls him the means of atonement for our sins, and Hebrews says he came to make atonement for the sins of the people. Galatians 3 verse 13 says he became a curse for us, quoting the law that anyone hanged on a tree is cursed. Two threads run together, substitution in the words for us and concerning our sins, and the bearing of judgment in the guilt offering, the crushing, the mercy seat, and the curse. There is one honest soft spot. The atonement word group can be read either as turning away anger or as cleansing sin, because it can name a place or object. The cleansing reading is real, but the same verb in Luke 18 verse 13 is a plea for God to be appeased, which tips the balance toward the fuller sense. First John 4 verse 10 anchors all of this in God's love. The evidence spans the law, the prophets, and several letters, so the verdict is affirmed with high confidence.
